claim: Inhibitors targeting the RTK/Ras/MAPK pathway have led to clinical responses in lung and other cancers.
source: Inhibitors that target the receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK)/Ras/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway have led to clinical responses in lung and other cancers, but some patients fail to respond and in those that do resistance inevitably occurs (Balak et al., 2006; Kosaka et al., 2006; Rudin et al., 2013; Wagle et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Balak et al., 2006; Kosaka et al., 2006; Rudin et al., 2013; Wagle et al., 2011).

claim: Some patients fail to respond to RTK/Ras/MAPK pathway inhibitors and in those that do resistance inevitably occurs.
source: Inhibitors that target the receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK)/Ras/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway have led to clinical responses in lung and other cancers, but some patients fail to respond and in those that do resistance inevitably occurs (Balak et al., 2006; Kosaka et al., 2006; Rudin et al., 2013; Wagle et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Balak et al., 2006; Kosaka et al., 2006; Rudin et al., 2013; Wagle et al., 2011).

claim: CRISPR-Cas9 gene deletion screens were performed in the setting of BRAF, MEK, EGFR, and ALK inhibition.
source: To understand intrinsic and acquired resistance to inhibition of MAPK signaling, we performed CRISPR-Cas9 gene deletion screens in the setting of BRAF, MEK, EGFR, and ALK inhibition.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Loss of KEAP1 modulated the response to BRAF, MEK, EGFR, and ALK inhibition in BRAF-, NRAS-, KRAS-, EGFR-, and ALK-mutant lung cancer cells.
source: Loss of KEAP1, a negative regulator of NFE2L2/NRF2, modulated the response to BRAF, MEK, EGFR, and ALK inhibition in BRAF-, NRAS-, KRAS-, EGFR-, and ALK-mutant lung cancer cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the CRISPR-Cas9 screens and validation experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: KEAP1 is a negative regulator of NFE2L2/NRF2.
source: Loss of KEAP1, a negative regulator of NFE2L2/NRF2, modulated the response to BRAF, MEK, EGFR, and ALK inhibition in BRAF-, NRAS-, KRAS-, EGFR-, and ALK-mutant lung cancer cells.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the KEAP1/NRF2 pathway.

claim: Treatment with inhibitors targeting the RTK/MAPK pathway increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) in cells with intact KEAP1.
source: Treatment with inhibitors targeting the RTK/MAPK pathway increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) in cells with intact KEAP1, and loss of KEAP1 abrogated this increase.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from DCFDA assays shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of KEAP1 abrogated the increase in ROS induced by RTK/MAPK pathway inhibitors.
source: Treatment with inhibitors targeting the RTK/MAPK pathway increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) in cells with intact KEAP1, and loss of KEAP1 abrogated this increase.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from DCFDA assays shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of KEAP1 altered cell metabolism to allow cells to proliferate in the absence of MAPK signaling.
source: In addition, loss of KEAP1 altered cell metabolism to allow cells to proliferate in the absence of MAPK signaling.
evidence: Supported by metabolite profiling data shown in Figure 4B-D and Supplementary file 3, as well as gene expression data in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Alterations in the KEAP1/NRF2 pathway may promote survival in the presence of multiple inhibitors targeting the RTK/Ras/MAPK pathway.
source: These observations suggest that alterations in the KEAP1/NRF2 pathway may promote survival in the presence of multiple inhibitors targeting the RTK/Ras/MAPK pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The RTK/MAPK pathway plays an important role in the development of lung and other cancers.
source: The receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK)/ mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway plays an important role in the development of lung and other cancers, with the frequent occurrence of mutations or copy number alterations in multiple nodes of this pathway (Ding et al., 2008; Imielinski et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Ding et al., 2008; Imielinski et al., 2012).

claim: Mutations or copy number alterations in multiple nodes of the RTK/MAPK pathway occur frequently in lung and other cancers.
source: The receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK)/ mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway plays an important role in the development of lung and other cancers, with the frequent occurrence of mutations or copy number alterations in multiple nodes of this pathway (Ding et al., 2008; Imielinski et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Ding et al., 2008; Imielinski et al., 2012).

claim: Single-agent therapy targeting the RTK/MAPK pathway has had limited clinical success.
source: However, single-agent therapy targeting this pathway has had limited clinical success.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by the context of the subsequent sentences discussing resistance.

claim: BRAF and EGFR inhibitors can produce dramatic responses temporarily.
source: While BRAF and EGFR inhibitors can produce dramatic responses temporarily, acquired resistance inevitably occurs in lung and other cancers (Balak et al., 2006; Kosaka et al., 2006; Rudin et al., 2013; Wagle et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Balak et al., 2006; Kosaka et al., 2006; Rudin et al., 2013; Wagle et al., 2011).

claim: Acquired resistance inevitably occurs to BRAF and EGFR inhibitors in lung and other cancers.
source: While BRAF and EGFR inhibitors can produce dramatic responses temporarily, acquired resistance inevitably occurs in lung and other cancers (Balak et al., 2006; Kosaka et al., 2006; Rudin et al., 2013; Wagle et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Balak et al., 2006; Kosaka et al., 2006; Rudin et al., 2013; Wagle et al., 2011).

claim: Many tumors exhibit intrinsic resistance to BRAF and EGFR inhibitors.
source: In addition to this acquired resistance, many tumors also exhibit intrinsic resistance to these inhibitors (Corcoran et al., 2012; Prahallad et al., 2012), as well as to MEK inhibitors (Sun et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Corcoran et al., 2012; Prahallad et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2014).

claim: Many tumors exhibit intrinsic resistance to MEK inhibitors.
source: In addition to this acquired resistance, many tumors also exhibit intrinsic resistance to these inhibitors (Corcoran et al., 2012; Prahallad et al., 2012), as well as to MEK inhibitors (Sun et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Sun et al., 2014).

claim: A general theme of resistance to targeted therapies is activation of the RTK/MAPK pathway by alternative mechanisms.
source: Several studies have now shown that a general theme of resistance to these targeted therapies is activation of the RTK/MAPK pathway by alternative mechanisms.
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings from multiple studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Feedback activation of EGFR causes intrinsic resistance to BRAF inhibition in colon cancer.
source: For example feedback activation of EGFR has been shown to cause intrinsic resistance to BRAF inhibition in colon cancer (Corcoran et al., 2012; Prahallad et al., 2012), and resistance to BRAF inhibition in melanoma can be caused by reactivation of the MAPK pathway by RTKs, NRAS, or COT (Johannessen et al., 2010; Nazarian et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Corcoran et al., 2012; Prahallad et al., 2012).

claim: Resistance to BRAF inhibition in melanoma can be caused by reactivation of the MAPK pathway by RTKs, NRAS, or COT.
source: For example feedback activation of EGFR has been shown to cause intrinsic resistance to BRAF inhibition in colon cancer (Corcoran et al., 2012; Prahallad et al., 2012), and resistance to BRAF inhibition in melanoma can be caused by reactivation of the MAPK pathway by RTKs, NRAS, or COT (Johannessen et al., 2010; Nazarian et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Johannessen et al., 2010; Nazarian et al., 2010).

claim: Transcriptional induction of ERBB3 causes intrinsic resistance to MEK inhibition in KRAS-mutant lung cancers.
source: In lung cancer, transcriptional induction of ERBB3 causes intrinsic resistance to MEK inhibition in KRAS-mutant cancers (Sun et al., 2014), and acquired resistance to EGFR inhibitors was found to result from amplification of MET (Engelman et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Sun et al., 2014).

claim: Acquired resistance to EGFR inhibitors results from amplification of MET.
source: In lung cancer, transcriptional induction of ERBB3 causes intrinsic resistance to MEK inhibition in KRAS-mutant cancers (Sun et al., 2014), and acquired resistance to EGFR inhibitors was found to result from amplification of MET (Engelman et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Engelman et al., 2007).

claim: These findings highlight the importance of maintaining RTK/MAPK signaling in lung and other cancers.
source: These findings highlight the importance of maintaining RTK/MAPK signaling in lung and other cancers and also suggest redundancy among different genetic alterations in this pathway.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies on resistance mechanisms.

claim: There is redundancy among different genetic alterations in the RTK/MAPK pathway.
source: These findings highlight the importance of maintaining RTK/MAPK signaling in lung and other cancers and also suggest redundancy among different genetic alterations in this pathway.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies showing multiple mechanisms of resistance.

claim: Combination therapy may hold more promise for treating tumors with alterations in the RTK/MAPK pathway.
source: Due to the many ways that cancers can acquire resistance to single therapies targeting the RTK/MAPK pathway, combination therapy may hold more promise for treating tumors with alterations in this pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the inference that multiple resistance mechanisms necessitate combination approaches.

claim: Patients with EGFR- and ALK-mutant lung cancer often respond to EGFR and ALK inhibitors.
source: While patients with EGFR- and ALK-mutant lung cancer do often respond to EGFR and ALK inhibitors, these responses are temporary, as acquired resistance inevitably develops (Tang et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Tang et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2015).

claim: Responses to EGFR and ALK inhibitors in EGFR- and ALK-mutant lung cancer are temporary.
source: While patients with EGFR- and ALK-mutant lung cancer do often respond to EGFR and ALK inhibitors, these responses are temporary, as acquired resistance inevitably develops (Tang et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Tang et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2015).

claim: Acquired resistance inevitably develops to EGFR and ALK inhibitors in EGFR- and ALK-mutant lung cancer.
source: While patients with EGFR- and ALK-mutant lung cancer do often respond to EGFR and ALK inhibitors, these responses are temporary, as acquired resistance inevitably develops (Tang et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Tang et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2015).

claim: Responses have been reported in some patients in on-going clinical trials testing MEK and BRAF inhibitors in KRAS- and BRAF-mutant lung cancer.
source: Likewise, in on-going clinical trials testing MEK and BRAF inhibitors in KRAS- and BRAF-mutant lung cancer, responses have been reported in some patients (Blumenschein et al., 2015; Hyman et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Blumenschein et al., 2015; Hyman et al., 2015).

claim: Both intrinsic and acquired resistance limits efficacy of MEK and BRAF inhibitors in KRAS- and BRAF-mutant lung cancer.
source: However, it is clear that both intrinsic and acquired resistance limits efficacy of these inhibitors.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field based on clinical trial results.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9 drug resistance screens were performed in five cancer cell lines with different alterations in the RTK/Ras/MAPK pathway.
source: To prospectively identify mechanisms of resistance to EGFR, ALK, BRAF, and MEK inhibition in lung cancer, we performed CRISPR-Cas9 drug resistance screens in five cancer cell lines with different alterations in the RTK/Ras/MAPK pathway.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: A number of genes whose deletion confers cell survival in the context of RTK/Ras/MAPK inhibition were identified.
source: We identified a number of genes whose deletion confers cell survival in these contexts, and focused on KEAP1, as loss of this gene modulated the response to targeted therapies in multiple contexts.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the CRISPR-Cas9 screens described in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of KEAP1 modulated the response to targeted therapies in multiple contexts.
source: We identified a number of genes whose deletion confers cell survival in these contexts, and focused on KEAP1, as loss of this gene modulated the response to targeted therapies in multiple contexts.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the CRISPR-Cas9 screens and validation experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Three genome scale screens were performed with the MEK inhibitor trametinib in NRAS-mutant, BRAF-mutant, and KRAS-mutant lung cancer cell lines.
source: In the first set (Figure 1A), we performed three genome scale screens with the MEK inhibitor trametinib, in the NRAS-mutant lung cancer cell line H1299 (NRASQ61K), the BRAF-mutant lung cancer cell line HCC364 (BRAFV600E), and the KRAS-mutant lung cancer cell line CALU1 (KRASG12C).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental design.

claim: One screen was performed in HCC364 cells treated with the BRAF inhibitor vemurafenib.
source: One additional screen was performed in HCC364 cells treated with the BRAF inhibitor vemurafenib.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental design.

claim: The GeCKO v2 library was introduced into Cas9-expressing cells to perform genome scale screens.
source: To perform genome scale screens, we introduced the GeCKO v2 library (Shalem et al., 2014) into Cas9-expressing cells, selected cells that incorporated the sgRNAs and allowed genome editing to occur over one week.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental method.

claim: The lowest concentration of drug that inhibited ERK phosphorylation and resulted in proliferative arrest or death was used in the screens.
source: We used the lowest concentration of drug that inhibited ERK phosphorylation and resulted in proliferative arrest or death (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental design, with supporting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Several of the genes that scored in these screens also scored in a previous vemurafenib resistance screen in BRAF-mutant melanoma.
source: Several of the genes that scored in these screens also scored in a previous vemurafenib resistance screen in BRAF-mutant melanoma (Shalem et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior literature (Shalem et al., 2014).

claim: NF1, a negative regulator of Ras/MAPK signaling, scored in the screens.
source: As expected, several genes in the MAPK pathway scored, including NF1, a negative regulator of Ras/MAPK signaling, and DUSP1, a dual-specificity phosphatase that inhibits ERK.
evidence: This is a finding from the CRISPR-Cas9 screens shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: DUSP1, a dual-specificity phosphatase that inhibits ERK, scored in the screens.
source: As expected, several genes in the MAPK pathway scored, including NF1, a negative regulator of Ras/MAPK signaling, and DUSP1, a dual-specificity phosphatase that inhibits ERK.
evidence: This is a finding from the CRISPR-Cas9 screens shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Several positive regulators of p38/JNK MAPK signaling scored in the screens.
source: We also found several positive regulators of p38/JNK MAPK signaling, suggesting that these other MAPK pathways may play a pro-apoptotic or anti-proliferative role in these cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the CRISPR-Cas9 screens shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: p38/JNK MAPK pathways may play a pro-apoptotic or anti-proliferative role in these cells.
source: We also found several positive regulators of p38/JNK MAPK signaling, suggesting that these other MAPK pathways may play a pro-apoptotic or anti-proliferative role in these cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that positive regulators of p38/JNK scored in the screens.

claim: PTEN, a negative regulator of PI3K/AKT signaling, scored in the screens.
source: PTEN, a negative regulator of PI3K/AKT signaling, and TSC1 and TSC2, negative regulators of mTOR signaling, also scored, suggesting that increased signaling through the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway compensates for loss of Ras/MAPK signaling.
evidence: This is a finding from the CRISPR-Cas9 screens shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: TSC1 and TSC2, negative regulators of mTOR signaling, scored in the screens.
source: PTEN, a negative regulator of PI3K/AKT signaling, and TSC1 and TSC2, negative regulators of mTOR signaling, also scored, suggesting that increased signaling through the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway compensates for loss of Ras/MAPK signaling.
evidence: This is a finding from the CRISPR-Cas9 screens shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Increased signaling through the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway compensates for loss of Ras/MAPK signaling.
source: PTEN, a negative regulator of PI3K/AKT signaling, and TSC1 and TSC2, negative regulators of mTOR signaling, also scored, suggesting that increased signaling through the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway compensates for loss of Ras/MAPK signaling.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that negative regulators of PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling scored in the screens.

claim: Several genes that are components of histone acetyltransferase (HAT) complexes scored in the screens.
source: In addition to these expected pathways, several of the genes that scored are components of histone acetyltransferase (HAT) complexes or of the Mediator complex.
evidence: This is a finding from the CRISPR-Cas9 screens shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Several genes that are components of the Mediator complex scored in the screens.
source: In addition to these expected pathways, several of the genes that scored are components of histone acetyltransferase (HAT) complexes or of the Mediator complex.
evidence: This is a finding from the CRISPR-Cas9 screens shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Several genes whose products are components of E3 ubiquitin ligase complexes scored in the screens.
source: There were also several genes whose products are components of E3 ubiquitin ligase complexes.
evidence: This is a finding from the CRISPR-Cas9 screens shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Multiple transcription factors scored in the screens.
source: Multiple transcription factors scored, as well as general transcription machinery genes.
evidence: This is a finding from the CRISPR-Cas9 screens shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: General transcription machinery genes scored in the screens.
source: Multiple transcription factors scored, as well as general transcription machinery genes.
evidence: This is a finding from the CRISPR-Cas9 screens shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Multiple genes involved in Rho signaling scored in the screens.
source: Other functional categories for which multiple genes scored include Rho signaling and histidine post-translational modifications.
evidence: This is a finding from the CRISPR-Cas9 screens shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Multiple genes involved in histidine post-translational modifications scored in the screens.
source: Other functional categories for which multiple genes scored include Rho signaling and histidine post-translational modifications.
evidence: This is a finding from the CRISPR-Cas9 screens shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: KEAP1 was the only gene that scored highly in all four genome scale screens.
source: We noted that KEAP1, a substrate adaptor protein that targets NFE2L2/NRF2 for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, was the only gene that scored highly in all four genome scale screens (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the CRISPR-Cas9 screens shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: KEAP1 is a substrate adaptor protein that targets NFE2L2/NRF2 for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation.
source: We noted that KEAP1, a substrate adaptor protein that targets NFE2L2/NRF2 for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, was the only gene that scored highly in all four genome scale screens (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the KEAP1/NRF2 pathway.

claim: A focused sgRNA library comprised of druggable targets was used to screen HCC827 cells treated with erlotinib and MGH-065 cells treated with crizotinib or LDK-378.
source: This library was used to screen HCC827 cells (EGFRΔ746-750) treated with the EGFR inhibitor erlotinib, and the patient-derived ALK-mutant line MGH-065 treated with the ALK inhibitors crizotinib or LDK-378 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental design.

claim: Loss of KEAP1 promoted survival in the presence of EGFR and ALK inhibitors.
source: Notably, loss of KEAP1 also promoted survival in the presence of EGFR and ALK inhibitors (Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the focused sgRNA library screens shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Loss of KEAP1 was found to modulate the response to multiple targeted therapeutics in different genetic contexts using two independent sgRNA libraries.
source: Thus, loss of KEAP1 was found to modulate the response to multiple targeted therapeutics in different genetic contexts using two independent sgRNA libraries.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from both the genome-scale and focused sgRNA library screens.

claim: KEAP1 knockout decreased sensitivity to afatinib treatment in NCI-H1975 cells.
source: KEAP1KO decreased sensitivity to afatinib treatment in NCI-H1975 (EGFRL858R/T790M) cells and to crizotinib treatment in NCI-H3122 (EML4-ALK) cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal violet assays in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: KEAP1 knockout decreased sensitivity to crizotinib treatment in NCI-H3122 cells.
source: KEAP1KO decreased sensitivity to afatinib treatment in NCI-H1975 (EGFRL858R/T790M) cells and to crizotinib treatment in NCI-H3122 (EML4-ALK) cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal violet assays in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Loss of KEAP1 caused a shift in the IC50 of erlotinib in HCC827 cells.
source: In short-term dose response experiments, loss of KEAP1 also caused a shift in the IC50 of erlotinib in HCC827 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is shown in the dose response curves in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: KEAP1 knockout did not restore ERK activation.
source: Unlike many other reported mechanisms of resistance to inhibitors of the RTK/Ras/MAPK pathway (Rudin et al., 2013; Wagle et al., 2011; Corcoran et al., 2012; Prahallad et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2014; Johannessen et al., 2010; Nazarian et al., 2010), we found that KEAP1KO did not restore ERK activation (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating that KEAP1KO does not decrease sensitivity by reactivating the MAPK pathway.
evidence: This is shown in the immunoblots in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: KEAP1 knockout does not decrease sensitivity by reactivating the MAPK pathway.
source: Unlike many other reported mechanisms of resistance to inhibitors of the RTK/Ras/MAPK pathway (Rudin et al., 2013; Wagle et al., 2011; Corcoran et al., 2012; Prahallad et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2014; Johannessen et al., 2010; Nazarian et al., 2010), we found that KEAP1KO did not restore ERK activation (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating that KEAP1KO does not decrease sensitivity by reactivating the MAPK pathway.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that ERK activation is not restored in KEAP1 knockout cells.

claim: Loss of KEAP1 did not affect expression of the pro-apoptotic protein BIM.
source: Loss of KEAP1 also did not affect expression of the pro-apoptotic protein BIM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the immunoblots in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Loss of KEAP1 did not generally promote survival by inhibiting apoptosis.
source: We concluded that loss of KEAP1 did not re-activate MAPK signaling or generally promote survival by inhibiting apoptosis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observations that ERK activation is not restored and BIM expression is not affected.

claim: KEAP1 knockout led to increased NRF2 protein levels.
source: As expected, we found that KEAP1KO led to increased NRF2 protein levels (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in the immunoblots in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: KEAP1 loss no longer promoted survival when NRF2 was also lost.
source: To determine if increased NRF2 levels were necessary for KEAP1 loss to modulate drug sensitivity, we knocked out both KEAP1 and NRF2 in HCC827 cells. KEAP1 loss no longer promoted survival when NRF2 was also lost (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal violet assays in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Increased NRF2 levels are necessary for KEAP1 loss to modulate drug sensitivity.
source: To determine if increased NRF2 levels were necessary for KEAP1 loss to modulate drug sensitivity, we knocked out both KEAP1 and NRF2 in HCC827 cells. KEAP1 loss no longer promoted survival when NRF2 was also lost (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that KEAP1 loss does not promote survival when NRF2 is also lost.

claim: Overexpression of wildtype NRF2 led to an increase in cell survival in the presence of multiple drugs.
source: To determine if increased NRF2 levels were sufficient to promote survival, we overexpressed wildtype NRF2 or two different NRF2 mutants (G31R or D29H), which contain mutations in the KEAP1 binding domain. Overexpression of wildtype NRF2 led to an increase in cell survival in the presence of multiple drugs.
evidence: This is shown in the crystal violet assays in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Overexpression of NRF2 G31R or D29H resulted in higher NRF2 protein levels and increased resistance to trametinib, vemurafenib, and erlotinib.
source: Overexpression of NRF2G31R or NRF2D29H resulted in higher NRF2 protein levels and increased resistance to trametinib, vemurafenib, and erlotinib (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that elevated NRF2 levels in KEAP1KO cells mediates resistance.
evidence: This is shown in the crystal violet assays and immunoblots in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Elevated NRF2 levels in KEAP1 knockout cells mediate resistance.
source: Overexpression of NRF2G31R or NRF2D29H resulted in higher NRF2 protein levels and increased resistance to trametinib, vemurafenib, and erlotinib (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that elevated NRF2 levels in KEAP1KO cells mediates resistance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that NRF2 overexpression increases resistance.

claim: CALU1 cells harbor a KEAP1 P128L mutation.
source: Although CALU1 cells harbor a KEAP1P128L mutation, this mutation has not been reported in the cBioPortal or COSMIC (Cerami et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2013; Forbes et al., 2015), and NRF2 levels increased upon KEAP1 knockout (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the regulation of NRF2 by KEAP1 is intact in these cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the genetic background of the CALU1 cell line.

claim: The KEAP1 P128L mutation has not been reported in the cBioPortal or COSMIC.
source: Although CALU1 cells harbor a KEAP1P128L mutation, this mutation has not been reported in the cBioPortal or COSMIC (Cerami et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2013; Forbes et al., 2015), and NRF2 levels increased upon KEAP1 knockout (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the regulation of NRF2 by KEAP1 is intact in these cells.
evidence: This is based on database searches in cBioPortal and COSMIC (Cerami et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2013; Forbes et al., 2015).

claim: The regulation of NRF2 by KEAP1 is intact in CALU1 cells.
source: Although CALU1 cells harbor a KEAP1P128L mutation, this mutation has not been reported in the cBioPortal or COSMIC (Cerami et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2013; Forbes et al., 2015), and NRF2 levels increased upon KEAP1 knockout (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the regulation of NRF2 by KEAP1 is intact in these cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that NRF2 levels increased upon KEAP1 knockout in CALU1 cells.

claim: Restoring wildtype KEAP1 expression in A549 cells increased their sensitivity to trametinib.
source: We also found that restoring wildtype KEAP1 expression in A549 cells, which are KRAS-mutant and KEAP1-null, increased their sensitivity to trametinib.
evidence: This is shown in the crystal violet assays in Figure 2F.

claim: A549 cells are KRAS-mutant and KEAP1-null.
source: We also found that restoring wildtype KEAP1 expression in A549 cells, which are KRAS-mutant and KEAP1-null, increased their sensitivity to trametinib.
evidence: This is a statement about the genetic background of the A549 cell line.

claim: Expression of the KEAP1 G333C mutant failed to alter trametinib sensitivity in A549 cells.
source: In contrast, expression of the KEAP1G333C mutant, which does not regulate NRF2, failed to alter trametinib sensitivity (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal violet assays in Figure 2F.

claim: The KEAP1 G333C mutant does not regulate NRF2.
source: In contrast, expression of the KEAP1G333C mutant, which does not regulate NRF2, failed to alter trametinib sensitivity (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the KEAP1 G333C mutant.

claim: Increased NRF2 levels upon loss of KEAP1 modulate sensitivity to therapies targeting the RTK/MAPK pathway.
source: Together these observations suggest that increased NRF2 levels upon loss of KEAP1 modulates sensitivity to therapies targeting the RTK/MAPK pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments showing that NRF2 is necessary and sufficient for KEAP1 loss to modulate drug sensitivity.

claim: Loss of KEAP1 has previously been reported to confer resistance to several chemotherapeutics.
source: Loss of KEAP1 has previously been reported to confer resistance to several chemotherapeutics (Ohta et al., 2008; Shibata et al., 2008a; Wang et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Ohta et al., 2008; Shibata et al., 2008a; Wang et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2010).

claim: KEAP1/NRF2 and the MAPK pathway are mechanistically linked.
source: However, it is also clear that KEAP1/NRF2 and the MAPK pathway are mechanistically linked (DeNicola et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (DeNicola et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2009).

claim: Ras/MAPK/Jun signaling increased expression of NRF2 mRNA and NRF2 target genes.
source: A prior report demonstrated that Ras/MAPK/Jun signaling increased expression of NRF2 mRNA and NRF2 target genes (DeNicola et al., 2011), so we hypothesized that drug treatment would decrease expression of NRF2 mRNA and NRF2-regulated target genes.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (DeNicola et al., 2011).
